name: Standard headroom (moving image)
definition: Small gap between top of head and top frame edge; eyes near the upper third line in 16:9, near 0.35-0.40 of height in 9:16.
how: Frame so the eye line sits ~1/3 from top (16:9). In 9:16 put eyes at 35-40% from top so the face clears the top UI strip (top 14% unsafe for text, faces are fine). Re-check headroom after every push-in: headroom must shrink as shot size tightens.
purpose: Keeps attention on the face without wasted space or cramped feel.
avoid_when: you want the character to feel crushed or small (use comp.headroom_excess or comp.headroom_cut)

examples.note: well-framed shot sits just above the head with eyes near the upper thirds line; applies to vertical too except in creative moments

ai_image_prompt: medium close-up, eyes on the upper third, small headroom, face fully in frame
ai_video_prompt: locked-off medium close-up, consistent small headroom, subject stays framed as she speaks
common_mistakes: same headroom on wide and close shots
eyes centred vertically (dead middle) in a 9:16 CU
AI crop cutting the chin while leaving big empty top
check: Draw a line at 1/3 (16:9) or 0.38 (9:16) height: eyes within +/-5% of it; no more than ~1 head-height of air above in MS.

name: Cut-forehead tight close-up
definition: Top frame line cuts through the forehead/hair in a CU or ECU so the eyes sit higher and the face fills the frame.
how: In a CU, keep the chin, sacrifice the top of the head; eyes still near the upper third. In 9:16 a 16:9-style CU already crops this way (Clayton: ~4/5 of screen).
purpose: Intensity, intimacy, pressure.
avoid_when: calm informational talking head
when the hairstyle/hat/glasses top bar is the product detail
ai_image_prompt: tight close-up, frame cuts across the forehead, eyes in upper third, chin included
ai_video_prompt: slow push-in from close-up to tight close-up cropping the top of the head, eyes stay on the upper third
common_mistakes: cutting the chin instead of the forehead
cutting the eyewear top rim when the glasses are the product
check: Chin visible; eyes not below centre; product edges not amputated.

name: Excess headroom / subject low in frame
definition: Deliberately large empty space above the subject.
how: Place the figure in the bottom quarter; let sky, ceiling, rain or water fill the top. Strongest in 9:16 (Clayton: expanse above head shows vulnerability to the natural world).
purpose: Isolation, smallness, being overwhelmed.
avoid_when: dialogue coverage (reads as error)
text must sit in the empty top 14% (UI covers it)

examples.note: individual placed at the bottom of a vertical screen walking through rain or snow indicates vulnerability

ai_image_prompt: small figure at the bottom of the frame, vast empty sky above, lots of negative space
ai_video_prompt: static wide, tiny figure walks at the bottom of the frame, huge empty sky above
common_mistakes: used without motivation so it reads as bad framing
check: Is the emptiness about the character's state? If not, reframe.

name: Look room (nose room)
definition: Extra space on the side the subject faces.
how: Place a profile/three-quarter face on the side opposite to its gaze (looking right -> subject left of centre). In 9:16 there is little width: use a wider lens, a 'rule of fifths' offset, or turn the eyeline more toward camera.
purpose: Lets the viewer see/anticipate what the character attends to; supports eyeline matches in editing.
avoid_when: you want unease or blocked future (use comp.short_side)

examples.note: inward bias: viewers prefer objects facing into the frame, not out

ai_image_prompt: three-quarter profile facing frame right, subject placed on the left third, open space in front of the face
ai_video_prompt: medium shot, character on the left facing right toward open space, she turns her head slowly right
common_mistakes: face pressed against the frame edge it looks at
in 9:16, centring a profile so the look room vanishes
check: Gaze side has more space than the back-of-head side.

name: Lead room for movement
definition: Space ahead of a moving subject in the direction of travel; camera leads, subject trails.
how: Pan/track so the mover stays 1/3 from the trailing edge. In 9:16 avoid long lateral moves; turn X-axis action into a diagonal toward/away from camera (comp.diagonal_x_to_z).
purpose: Viewer sees where the subject is going; motion feels free.
use_when: walks, runs, vehicles, product sliding into frame
avoid_when: chase where the threat behind matters (leave space behind instead)

examples.note: with any camera movement create lead space ahead of the subject in the direction of movement
inward bias weakens as implied motion speed increases; motion direction can override facing direction

ai_image_prompt: cyclist on the left third riding toward the right, open road ahead in frame
ai_video_prompt: tracking shot alongside, the walker stays on the left third with open space ahead as the camera leads
common_mistakes: camera lags so the subject hits the leading edge
AI video drifts the subject to centre mid-shot
check: Pause at 3 points in the shot: leading space >= trailing space each time.

name: Short-siding (closed frame)
definition: Subject placed on the side it faces, with empty space behind the head.
how: Looking right -> place the face on the right third; leave the space behind. Hold longer than feels comfortable.
purpose: Unease, blocked future, something behind them, alienation.
avoid_when: neutral dialogue coverage
early in a scene before the audience knows the framing is deliberate

examples.note: commonly attributed to Mr. Robot's cinematography; not checked against a source this session

ai_image_prompt: woman pressed against the right edge of frame looking right, large empty wall behind her head
ai_video_prompt: static medium close-up, character at the right edge facing the edge, empty space behind her, a shadow moves across the empty space
common_mistakes: mixing short-side and normal look room randomly in one conversation (reads as error)
check: Is it consistent for that character/beat and motivated by the story?

name: Centred hero (single subject)
definition: Subject dead centre, often frontal and symmetrical.
how: Centre horizontally; set vertical position by headroom; keep background symmetrical or simple. For product: centre the frame, put text above/below inside the safe zone.
purpose: Clarity, authority, formality, a product 'portrait'.
use_when: vertical 9:16 talking head (no width for thirds anyway)
avoid_when: a scene needs implied off-screen space or anticipation

examples.note: centre was the most preferred position for every object in every facing direction (strongest for symmetric forward-facing objects)

ai_image_prompt: eyeglasses centred, front view, perfectly symmetrical composition, plain background
ai_video_prompt: centred symmetrical frame, slow push-in, subject stays exactly centred
common_mistakes: centring by habit in every shot so the cut rhythm has no variety
off by a few pixels — near-centre looks like a mistake
check: Overlay a vertical centre line: within 1% if meant to be centred.

name: Vertical (9:16) close-up framed to the chest/navel
definition: In 9:16 a 'close-up' that keeps emotional readability is framed lower (to chest or navel) than a 16:9 CU (to shoulders).
how: Bottom frame at chest for 'CU', navel for 'MCU-feel'; eyes ~38% from top; hands can enter frame (hand-to-face objects like glasses suit vertical).
purpose: Avoid accidental ECU when copying 16:9 shot sizes into 9:16.
use_when: Reels/TikTok dialogue, talking head, try-on of glasses
avoid_when: you really want an ECU detail

examples.note: a horizontal close-up fills ~half the screen; the same framing in vertical fills ~4/5 and reads as big/extreme CU; vertical CU may be framed down to the navel

ai_image_prompt: vertical 9:16 portrait, framed from head to chest, hands raising glasses to the face, eyes at upper 40%
ai_video_prompt: vertical 9:16, framed head to chest, she lifts the glasses up to her face and puts them on
common_mistakes: using 16:9 shot-size names unchanged
eyes in the middle of the 9:16 frame
check: Face height <= ~45% of frame height for a 'CU' in 9:16.

name: Rule of fifths (vertical offset)
definition: In a 9:16 frame place the subject on the 1/5 or 4/5 vertical line to regain look room.
how: Divide width into fifths; face on the 2/5 or 3/5 line is near-centre, 1/5 line is a bold offset (risky in UI side zones: keep 6% side margin).
purpose: Create look room in narrow frames.
use_when: two-person interplay staged in depth in vertical
avoid_when: faces would fall under the right-side TikTok/Reels buttons

examples.note: proposes a 'Rule of Fifths' for vertical; 'not for the faint-hearted'

ai_image_prompt: vertical frame, character placed near the left edge (one fifth in), looking right across the empty frame
ai_video_prompt: vertical 9:16, subject near the left edge looks across the frame to the right where a second character enters
common_mistakes: face under the right-side app buttons
offset for no story reason
check: Face fully inside the 6% side margin and outside the right-side icon column.

name: Turn lateral action into a diagonal (for 9:16)
definition: Move the camera so action that would cross the frame sideways travels diagonally toward or away from the lens.
how: Rotate the camera 30-60 deg off the line of action; or track with the subject if it must be lateral.
purpose: Keeps movement inside a narrow frame longer; adds depth.
use_when: walking, running, product sliding, vehicles in 9:16
avoid_when: sport/side-line action that only reads laterally (consider 16:9)

examples.note: horizontal action can become diagonal action by moving the camera so the angle bisects the Z/X axis

ai_image_prompt: vertical frame, person walking diagonally toward the camera from the far left background
ai_video_prompt: vertical 9:16, the man walks diagonally from far background left toward the camera, camera static
common_mistakes: subject exits the narrow frame in under a second
check: Subject stays in frame >= 1.5 s of movement.

name: Top/bottom dominance in 9:16
definition: Power is shown by vertical position: dominant entity high in frame, subordinate low.
how: Stack two subjects vertically, or place one figure low against a tall element (building, mountain, adult). Combine with low/high angle.
purpose: Status, power, challenge.
avoid_when: equal partners in a dialogue

examples.note: powerful character at the top of the screen, weaker at the bottom; Jack at the foot of the beanstalk

ai_image_prompt: vertical frame, tall adult looms in the top half, small child looks up from the bottom of the frame
ai_video_prompt: vertical 9:16, slow tilt up from a small figure at the bottom to a towering building filling the top
common_mistakes: claiming a fixed psychological law; it is a craft convention
check: Does the vertical order match who has power in this beat?

name: Frame within frame (doorway, window, mirror, screen)
definition: A shape inside the shot (door, window, arch, mirror, phone screen, glasses rim) frames the subject; in motion the inner frame can be revealed, entered or crossed.
how: Put the inner frame in the foreground or midground; light the subject brighter than the frame; let characters step into/out of it; dolly through it for a transition.
purpose: Focus, voyeurism, confinement, a story-within-story; ready-made vertical sub-frame inside 16:9.
use_when: eyewear: scene seen through the lens/rim
avoid_when: inner frame competes in brightness with the subject

examples.note: POV through a telescopic sight or rifle scope: the circular boundary makes the outer aspect ratio largely irrelevant

ai_image_prompt: view through a dark doorway, woman framed by the door edges in a bright room beyond
ai_video_prompt: camera slowly dollies forward through a dark doorway toward the woman in the bright room beyond
common_mistakes: inner frame not aligned/parallel (reads as accident)
too dark to read the frame edges on phones
check: Thumbnail at 10% size: is the inner frame still readable?

name: Staging in three depth zones
definition: Action arranged in foreground, midground and background in one shot so emphasis shifts without cutting.
how: Place a secondary figure or object large in the foreground, the main action in midground, a payoff or threat in the background. Move actors toward/away from camera to transfer emphasis; use light, focus and stillness of others to rank.
purpose: Fewer cuts, richer frames, clear gradation of emphasis.
use_when: shop scene: customer foreground, optician midground, product wall background
avoid_when: 9:16 frames too narrow for side-by-side zones (stack in depth along the lens axis instead)
AI video models that merge overlapping figures

examples.note: two-minute scene in two shots; later mortuary scene uses three depth zones; staging guides attention instead of cutting

examples.work: The Best Years of Our Lives (1946)
examples.note: Homer at the piano in the foreground while the consequential action is in a distant phone booth

ai_image_prompt: three layers: blurred shoulder of a customer in the foreground, optician holding glasses in the midground, glowing display wall in the background
ai_video_prompt: static shot in depth: foreground customer turns away, revealing the optician in the midground walking toward camera, display wall behind
common_mistakes: all three zones equally bright and sharp (no hierarchy)
depth zones but the eye path is not designed
check: Name the primary, secondary, tertiary element for each second of the shot.

name: Blocking and revealing
definition: A figure or object momentarily hides another; a small move opens a 'slot' that reveals it.
how: Plan the reveal moment on the beat; the blocker moves 20-40 cm, or the camera arcs slightly; keep other figures still.
purpose: Control what the audience sees and when, inside a shot.
use_when: product reveal from behind a hand/object
avoid_when: the hidden element is needed for comprehension earlier

examples.note: a patrolman restrains a man, opening a 'slot' to reveal another character; head-blocking masks a face to focus a reaction

ai_video_prompt: medium shot, a man in the foreground steps to the left, revealing the woman behind him who is staring at the camera
common_mistakes: reveal mistimed vs dialogue/music
AI video: blocker and hidden figure merge
check: Reveal frame lands within 2 frames of the intended beat.

name: Priming: plant in the background, pay off later
definition: An element shown small/secondary early becomes important later.
how: Show the object in background/edge of an early shot with mild emphasis (light, colour accent); later make it primary. Do not over-stress it.
purpose: Setup/payoff without exposition; product placement that feels earned.
use_when: story clips with a prop (glasses on a table)
avoid_when: very short ads where nothing can be held back

examples.note: a figure emerges out of focus behind Ben Wade, signalling the posse
Paula's robe primed then used for suspense; Bordwell: 'if you stress a secondary element too much, it becomes primary'

ai_image_prompt: cosy room, a pair of round glasses lying on the shelf in the background, small but catching a rim light
common_mistakes: plant so loud it becomes primary
plant forgotten in later shots (continuity)
check: Is the plant visible on a phone at 1x? Is it secondary in brightness/size?

name: Dirty single / OTS with foreground shoulder
definition: Single on one character with a slice of the other character's shoulder/head out of focus in the foreground.
how: Foreground shoulder occupies 10-25% of the frame edge on the side opposite the look room; keep it darker/softer than the subject.
purpose: Keeps the relationship and spatial layout present; adds an occlusion depth cue.
avoid_when: you want isolation (use a clean single)
ai_image_prompt: over-the-shoulder medium close-up, blurred dark shoulder in the left foreground, woman in focus facing camera-left
ai_video_prompt: over-the-shoulder shot, soft foreground shoulder, the woman in focus nods and answers
common_mistakes: foreground brighter than subject
crossing the 180 line between reverse shots
check: Foreground darker and softer; eyeline matches the reverse.

name: Negative space held in time
definition: Large empty area that stays empty (or is entered) over the duration of the shot.
how: Hold the shot 1-2 s longer than needed; optionally let something enter the empty area late.
purpose: Loneliness, anticipation, breathing room in a fast edit, room for text overlay.
use_when: title/text cards over image (put text in the empty area inside the safe zone)
avoid_when: hook seconds of a Reel (empty frames lose scroll)
ai_image_prompt: minimal composition, small subject in the lower left, large empty pale wall
ai_video_prompt: static shot, the empty right side of the frame stays empty, after a few seconds a shadow enters
common_mistakes: negative space under the platform UI where text will be covered
check: Empty area still inside safe zone if it will carry text.

name: One-point symmetry / corridor tunnel
definition: Symmetrical frame with converging lines to a central vanishing point; strong in vertical frames for corridors, stairs, roads.
how: Camera centred on the corridor axis, lens height mid-frame; subject on the axis.
purpose: Order, inevitability, forward motion; vertical frames suit corridors and stairs.
avoid_when: naturalistic scenes where it feels mannered

examples.note: corridors and stairways suit vertical ratio; straight roads lead the eye forward

ai_image_prompt: symmetrical one-point perspective corridor, vanishing point at centre, figure walking toward camera
ai_video_prompt: vertical 9:16, camera pushes slowly down a symmetrical corridor toward a figure at the vanishing point
common_mistakes: camera slightly off-axis (lines not mirrored)
check: Mirror the frame: lines should overlap.

name: Aspect ratio as story device (frame change)
definition: Changing the frame shape between periods/worlds or within a shot (pillarbox opening, letterbox closing).
how: Assign a ratio per world/time; or animate mattes to expand at an emotional release. In 9:16 delivery, simulate by masking (e.g., 1:1 window inside 9:16 opening to full).
purpose: Mark time/world; make release or confinement physical.
avoid_when: Reels where black bars waste feed space without a reason

examples.note: 1.37 for 1932, 1.85 modern, anamorphic widescreen for 1968: ratios 'tell viewers where they are in the timeline'
mostly 1:1, widens to 1.85 in a liberation/elation moment then returns to square

common_mistakes: ratio changes with no story logic
mattes covering subtitles/UI-safe text
check: Can you state the rule for every ratio change in one sentence?

name: Reels/TikTok safe-zone layout
definition: Keep text, logos and key detail out of platform UI zones in 9:16.
how: On 1080x1920 keep text/logos inside x 65-1015, y 269-1248 (Meta ads guide: top 14%, bottom 35%, sides 6%). TikTok: use its downloadable template (depends on caption length). Faces may enter UI zones; text may not.
purpose: Nothing important covered by captions, buttons, profile row.

examples.note: 14% top / 35% bottom / 6% sides kept free of text, logos, key elements

ai_image_prompt: vertical 9:16 composition with the subject in the upper-middle and calm empty space at the bottom third
common_mistakes: price/CTA in the bottom 35%
logo top-left inside the top 14% (profile row)
check: Overlay the safe-box PNG at QC (see TECH_SPEC_PRESETS spec.ig_reels_9x16).

name: Re-composing a 16:9 shot for 9:16
definition: Deriving a vertical version from a horizontal master by re-composition, not centre-cut.
how: Per shot: pick the subject's x-centre (face/eyes or product), crop 9:16 around it, animate the crop when the subject moves (keyframed pan), and replace two-shots side-by-side with alternating singles or a depth-staged re-shoot. Shoot/generate with 9:16 'protect' area if both versions are planned.
purpose: Keep look room, headroom and readability in both formats.
use_when: one story delivered to YouTube 16:9 and Reels 9:16
avoid_when: two-shots where both faces are essential at opposite edges (re-shoot/re-generate)
common_mistakes: static centre crop cutting one speaker
crop that follows every jitter (nauseating)
check: Every shot: subject's eyes inside the 9:16 crop; crop moves are eased and motivated.

name: Re-balancing as subjects move
definition: In moving images balance is temporal: the frame is re-balanced by actor moves, camera reframes or a new element entering.
how: Plan start and end compositions; let movement carry the frame from imbalanced (tension) to balanced (resolution) or the reverse.
purpose: Use composition change itself as an emotional beat (Block: contrast/affinity of space and movement).
use_when: beats that turn within one shot
avoid_when: very short cuts (<1 s) where nobody sees the change
ai_video_prompt: starts with the woman alone at the left edge of an empty frame, a friend walks in and stands on the right, balancing the frame
common_mistakes: only judging the first frame of a moving shot
check: Grab first/middle/last frame; each composition intended?
